_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla, typed out on the slip. Each lesson has two: "start" comes on as the lesson opens, and "check" is a short quiz once the lesson's check is done. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies" (none means a plain "Roger. Over."). A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. A letter from a fellow at the lighthouse on Destruction Island. Two thousand hours of fog on his log some years, and not one thunderclap all summer. Same summer we had six storms over the wheat. This week, why.

replies.back: Part of it. The sea, and what’s sitting on top of it.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. Questions. North wind down the Oregon coast all week in July. What does the sea at the beach do?

replies.back: Right. The top water drifts off to sea and the cold comes up from below.
Other way. The surface water goes offshore and cold water comes up to take its place.
It gets colder. The wind sends the top water out to sea, and the deep water rises.

turns.them: Why don’t the heaps grow over the summer beach?

replies.say: They hit the warm lid and stop.
replies.back: That’s it. Sinking air from the high keeps the top warm and the sea keeps the bottom cold.

replies.say: Not enough water in the air.
replies.back: Plenty of water down there; it’s foggy. What’s missing is a warm bottom under a cool top.
No. They stop at the lid a few hundred feet up.

turns.them: Last one. When does the coast get what thunder it does?

replies.say: Autumn and winter, behind the cold fronts.
replies.back: Right. Cold air over a warmer sea. Hail pellets and a clap or two. Seventy-three.
That’s when it’s least likely. Autumn and winter, behind the cold fronts.
Almost never. What there is comes in autumn and winter, behind the cold fronts.
